tools.name: mcp__7381ab3a-4726-4c34-8ffb-687452585236__get_meeting_transcript
tools.description: Get the verbatim transcript of a Granola meeting by ID; no summaries or notes. Returns up to 40000 characters per call by default (max_chars, up to 80000), cut at an utterance boundary with total_chars, truncated and next_offset reported. A page that splits an oversized utterance has ends_mid_utterance and the next starts_mid_utterance. With meeting_ids, meetings has one entry per requested ID in request order, with the single-read fields or an error. The batch shares 80000 characters: each meeting returns up to max_chars or an equal share of that, whichever is smaller. Pass offsets to continue several meetings in one call. An accessible meeting with no transcript returns transcript null (status "unavailable" for chunk reads) and transcript_unavailable with a reason: transcript_pending means retry in a few minutes; not_happened_yet means retry after the meeting; no_transcript and transcript_deleted are final. "Meeting not found" means the ID does not resolve or is not accessible. Transcript blocks separate audio source (Microphone/System audio) from speaker identity; mobile/imported transcripts may keep Speaker A/B labels. For native recordings, recording context identifies the document owner as the recorder, not necessarily the speaker; missing recorder data stays unknown. Needs a paid Granola plan. If it returns a paid-plan error, use the other meeting tools and say when their results lack the requested detail.

schema.name: mcp__7381ab3a-4726-4c34-8ffb-687452585236__get_meeting_transcript
schema.description: Get the verbatim transcript of a Granola meeting by ID; no summaries or notes. Returns up to 40000 characters per call by default (max_chars, up to 80000), cut at an utterance boundary with total_chars, truncated and next_offset reported. A page that splits an oversized utterance has ends_mid_utterance and the next starts_mid_utterance. With meeting_ids, meetings has one entry per requested ID in request order, with the single-read fields or an error. The batch shares 80000 characters: each meeting returns up to max_chars or an equal share of that, whichever is smaller. Pass offsets to continue several meetings in one call. An accessible meeting with no transcript returns transcript null (status "unavailable" for chunk reads) and transcript_unavailable with a reason: transcript_pending means retry in a few minutes; not_happened_yet means retry after the meeting; no_transcript and transcript_deleted are final. "Meeting not found" means the ID does not resolve or is not accessible. Transcript blocks separate audio source (Microphone/System audio) from speaker identity; mobile/imported transcripts may keep Speaker A/B labels. For native recordings, recording context identifies the document owner as the recorder, not necessarily the speaker; missing recorder data stays unknown. Needs a paid Granola plan. If it returns a paid-plan error, use the other meeting tools and say when their results lack the requested detail.

meeting_ids.description: Meeting UUIDs or public note IDs (max 10). With several IDs, offset applies to each meeting and the meetings share 80000 characters, so each returns up to max_chars or an equal share, whichever is smaller; use offsets to start meetings at different positions. A meeting that cannot be read gets an error entry and the others are still returned. Empty arrays are ignored.

note_ids.description: Alias for meeting_ids. If both are nonempty, they must refer to the same set of notes; order, duplicates, and UUID/public ID format may differ.

meeting_id.description: Alias for meeting_ids with a single meeting. Every ID argument provided must name the same meetings.

note_id.description: Alias for meeting_ids with a single meeting. Every ID argument provided must name the same meetings.

offset.description: Character offset; pass next_offset to continue, with the same include_timestamps as that page.

max_chars.description: Maximum size of the transcript field as sent (integer, at least 1,000), cut at the last utterance that fits; a page holds fewer transcript characters when the text needs JSON escaping. Defaults to 40000; larger requests are capped at 80000. Use next_offset to continue. Lower it if responses exceed your output limit.

include_timestamps.description: Prefix each reliably timed block with [m:ss], minutes:seconds since the transcript's earliest timed block, not clock time; that block can predate the meeting when recording started early. Applies to every page; chunk_ids reads always include them. Adds about 7 characters per block, and offset, next_offset and total_chars count the text as rendered with it, so keep the same value when continuing from next_offset. When no block has timing, no prefixes are added and timestamps_unavailable says so.

offsets.description: With meeting_ids only: character offset per meeting, keyed by meeting ID, e.g. {"<id>": 8000}. Pass each truncated meeting's next_offset to continue several transcripts in one call. Meetings not listed start at offset. Omit or pass {} when not needed.

chunk_ids.description: Read up to ten finalized transcript chunks instead of the full transcript. Use chunk IDs from search_transcripts, or [0] to browse from the beginning. IDs past the last chunk are skipped and listed in ignored_chunk_ids; if none of the IDs exist the status is out_of_range. Each chunk's transcript is verbatim text in the full read's format: one block per speaker turn, prefixed with [m:ss] (minutes:seconds since the transcript's earliest timed block, omitted when unknown) and the speaker label; preformatted transcripts keep their own text and labels. Also returns total_chunks and previous/next chunk IDs.

transcript_version.description: With chunk_ids, reuse the version from search or a previous chunk read. A changed status returns no chunks: search again or restart browsing without the old version. Omit chunk_ids and transcript_version for the existing full transcript read.

tools.name: mcp__7381ab3a-4726-4c34-8ffb-687452585236__get_meetings
tools.description: Read one or more Granola meetings by ID: private notes, AI summary, attendees, metadata and note URLs. Use it when you have meeting IDs from discovery results or note URLs; batch up to 10 IDs per call. Private notes appear only for meetings the user owns (status "empty": no text; "not_included": another user owns the note). meeting_at is the calendar event's scheduled start (created_at without an event), so it can differ from when the meeting was recorded. Invalid, missing and inaccessible IDs are reported separately; the other meetings are still returned. If the meetings would exceed 80000 characters, the last ones are left out and listed in omitted_meetings; read them in another call. The first meeting is always returned whole, so one long meeting can exceed 80000 characters. The note creator and participants are not necessarily the connected user: confirm the connected user's identity with get_account_info and match it to explicit ownership evidence before drafting in the user's voice or assigning them actions; first-person notes are not proof of the user's voice. Dated plans do not establish current progress. known_participants comes from the calendar invite, attendees added by hand, and the note creator; anyone else who spoke appears only in the notes and transcript. Does not return transcripts; notes can omit details that were discussed. If a detail is missing, get_meeting_transcript may have it on a paid Granola plan; if it returns a paid-plan error, say the detail is missing rather than conclude it was never discussed. Shared-screen screenshots appear in <attachments> with an ID, time offset and lossy description; for anything visual (designs, slides, charts, code), view them with get_meeting_attachment. Attached photos appear as <attachment type="photo"> without a description; view them with get_meeting_attachment. Keep at most 5 get_meetings calls in flight, and only for calls you already need. On a rate_limit error, retry only the failed call after retry_after_seconds, one at a time, and not when retryable is false.

tools.name: REDACTED
tools.description: Query Granola about the user's meetings in natural language. Returns an answer with inline markdown citation links (e.g. [[1]](url)) to the source meeting notes; keep them in your response so the user can verify it. The citation URL https://notes.granola.ai/d/<meeting_id> gives the ID to pass to get_meetings (meeting_ids). The answer is a summary that can leave out owners, numbers, dates and exact wording; when the question asks for those, read the cited meetings with get_meetings first. This tool is slow: an agent behind it searches and reads the user's notes. Prefer a faster tool when it can answer: - Meeting discovery tools: find meetings by date range - get_meetings: read notes for meetings whose IDs you already have - search_meetings: find meetings by keyword, participant or company Use it for what was discussed, decided or assigned across meetings, follow-ups and commitments, or when the user references their 'Granola notes'. When NOT to use: - Calendar scheduling or upcoming events - A specific meeting by ID: use get_meetings Transcripts need a paid Granola plan. If get_meeting_transcript returns a paid-plan error and results lack a detail, say so rather than conclude it was never discussed. Keep at most 15 query_granola_meetings calls in flight, and only for calls you already need. On a rate_limit error, retry only the failed call after retry_after_seconds, one at a time, and not when retryable is false.

tools.name: mcp__7381ab3a-4726-4c34-8ffb-687452585236__search_meetings
tools.description: Find the user's meetings by keyword, participant/company, date, or a combination. Keyword searches cover meeting titles, summaries and your private notes. They do not search transcripts: an empty result does not mean a term was never spoken in a meeting. Returns metadata only (title, date, participants, note headings), not what was said: read the relevant meetings with get_meetings before answering about their content, and use get_meetings directly for a meeting you already identified. With keywords or participant, results are ranked by relevance favouring recent meetings; with neither, newest first, defaulting to the last 7 days unless folder_id is set. Pages can be short or empty; continue with next_cursor while it is present. completion_status incomplete means continuation is unavailable: narrow the search. participant matches participant metadata (names, emails, companies, domains), not mentions in notes, as an AND filter with the other inputs; metadata can be incomplete. For broader questions about a person or company, also search their name plus the topic in keywords with participant omitted: internal discussions may hold the answer. Captures of the same calendar event are grouped, keeping the user's own note or else the newest; read other_ids in duplicate_recordings only for details the listed note lacks or when the user asks to compare attendees' notes. Use attended_only=true for 'my meetings'. list_meeting_folders gives folder_id values. Keyword matching is literal, so pass the user's words plus obvious synonyms. Meetings with viewable attachments carry an attachment_count attribute; get_meetings lists them. Keep at most 2 search_meetings calls in flight, and only for calls you already need. On a rate_limit error, retry only the failed call after retry_after_seconds, one at a time, and not when retryable is false.

cursor.description: Opaque next_cursor from the previous response. Omit filters to reuse them, or repeat the same filters. Omit cursor or pass an empty string for the first page. Cursors expire after 15 minutes.

folder_id.description: Only return meetings in this folder or its nested folders. Use list_meeting_folders to discover folder IDs.

workspace_only.description: Set to true only when the user explicitly asks for Team Space, public workspace, or workspace-visible meetings. Omit or set to false to search every meeting the user is allowed to access. Combines with folder_id and include_shared using AND.

keywords.description: Groups of words to search for in meeting titles, summaries, or your private notes. Transcript text is not searched. All words in one entry must appear within the same field, in any order or position. Entries are alternatives (OR): ["MCP write tools"] requires all three words; ["write tools", "write access"] matches either group. Pass at most 20 entries. Adjacent words in the supplied order get a relevance boost, but exact phrases are not required. A single comma-separated string is also accepted. Omit to browse meetings by date.

max_participants.description: Maximum attendees to list per meeting, besides the note creator. Omit to list everyone. Set a small value (e.g. 10) for broad ranges or large meetings to keep responses small. When attendees are left out, known_participants has total and omitted attributes, e.g. <known_participants total="250" omitted="240">.

participant.description: Filter by a whole name, email, company or domain in participant metadata, not a name prefix, nickname or part of an email address. Combines with keywords, dates, and folder using AND. Mentions in notes alone do not match; missing participant metadata can hide relevant meetings. For broader questions about their work, account status, decisions, issue resolution, or preparation, also search the person/company and topic in keywords without this filter to include internal discussions.

limit.description: Requested meetings per page (positive integer). Defaults to 30 and is capped at 100. Larger requests use the cap; use next_cursor to continue. Duplicates or inaccessible matches can make a page shorter.

attended_only.description: Only notes the user captured or where their email is listed as a creator or attendee, and upcoming calendar meetings the user is invited to or organised. Approximates attendance; defaults to false.

include_shared.description: Also search notes other people shared with the user. Defaults to true when omitted.

from_date.description: Only meetings on or after this ISO date or time, using calendar start when available, otherwise note creation. Dates and offsetless times use the user's timezone (UTC if unavailable); explicit offsets are respected, so for a day in another timezone give both bounds as times with that timezone's offset.

to_date.description: Only meetings on or before this ISO date or time. YYYY-MM-DD includes the whole day in the user's timezone (UTC if unavailable); explicit offsets are respected. Uses calendar start when available, otherwise note creation.

updated_after.description: Only notes whose summary or content changed after this ISO date or time; matching rows then show updated_at. Use it to pick up changes since a previous call. Combines with the other filters using AND; without from_date and to_date it covers all accessible meeting history (the last 30 days on the free plan) instead of the last 7 days. Offsetless values use the user's timezone (UTC if unavailable).

tools.name: mcp__7381ab3a-4726-4c34-8ffb-687452585236__search_transcripts
tools.description: Find specific words or quotes in accessible meeting transcripts in the active workspace. Returns ranked passages with approximate timestamps. Needs a paid Granola plan. If it returns a paid-plan error, use the other meeting tools. Supply meeting_ids when known, batching meetings that share the same terms and filters. Matching is literal, in the script and spelling the transcript uses; put alternative words and spellings in one keywords array, e.g. ["pricing", "price", "cost"], since no match can mean the term was written differently, not that nobody said it. For what a person or company said, use participant (names/companies) or attendee_emails/attendee_domains (invite list). participant is an AND filter on metadata that can be incomplete, so for broader questions also search their name and the topic in keywords without it. Known meetings with no indexed match are also searched in their current transcripts. Without meeting_ids, search relies on an asynchronously updated index and groups duplicate recordings; empty results do not prove a topic was never discussed. Pages can be short or empty; continue with next_cursor while it is present. If completion_status is incomplete, narrow the search or read known transcripts. Read surrounding dialogue with get_meeting_transcript using meeting_id, the passage's chunk_ids and transcript_version; adjacent chunk IDs continue, and omitting chunk_ids reads the whole conversation. counts is cumulative across pages; total_matching_chunks is a first-page estimate, null for direct search. Neither counts spoken mentions. Use another tool when: - The term is likely in the notes, or the user wants meetings about a topic: use search_meetings - You need the whole conversation: use get_meeting_transcript

tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': absolute path (no ~) to the built .app bundle (e.g. /Users/me/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/MyApp-abc123/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. import Foundation

/// Robustness to head movement (D42).
///
/// `Interference.mix` adds the head/face movement recorded in one take (typically a `_none` take:
/// turn, nod, look up, chew, swallow, smile) onto another, at a chosen strength. For small motions
/// the extra rotation rate and acceleration simply add, and the extra rotation composes onto the
/// attitude. That makes realistic "mouthing while moving" data out of real recordings, for testing
/// and, optionally, as noisy training copies.
public enum Interference {
    /// `alpha` scales the interference (1 = as recorded). `offset` shifts it in time (seconds).
    public static func mix(_ base: [MotionSample], with noise: [MotionSample], alpha: Double, offset: Double = 0) -> [MotionSample] {
        guard let b0 = base.first?.t, let n0 = noise.first?.t, let q0 = noise.first?.attitude, alpha != 0 else { return base }
        let nt = noise.map { $0.t - n0 }
        var j = 0
        return base.map { s in
            let t = s.t - b0 + offset
            while j + 1 < noise.count, nt[j + 1] <= t { j += 1 }
            guard t >= 0, t <= (nt.last ?? 0) else { return s }
            let n = noise[j]
            var out = s
            out.rotation = s.rotation + n.rotation * alpha
            out.accel = s.accel + n.accel * alpha
            let extra = Quat(rotationVector: (q0.conjugate * n.attitude).rotationVector * alpha)
            out.attitude = (s.attitude * extra).normalized
            out.gravity = extra.conjugate.rotate(s.gravity)
            out.pitch = s.pitch + (n.pitch - noise[0].pitch) * alpha
            out.yaw = s.yaw + remainder(n.yaw - noise[0].yaw, 2 * .pi) * alpha
            out.roll = s.roll + (n.roll - noise[0].roll) * alpha
            return out

import Foundation

/// Robustness to head movement (D42).
///
/// `Interference.mix` adds the head/face movement recorded in one take (typically a `_none` take:
/// turn, nod, look up, chew, swallow, smile) onto another, at a chosen strength. For small motions
/// the extra rotation rate and acceleration simply add, and the extra rotation composes onto the
/// attitude. That makes realistic "mouthing while moving" data out of real recordings, for testing
/// and, optionally, as noisy training copies.
public enum Interference {
    /// `alpha` scales the interference (1 = as recorded). `offset` shifts it in time (seconds).
    public static func mix(_ base: [MotionSample], with noise: [MotionSample], alpha: Double, offset: Double = 0) -> [MotionSample] {
        guard let b0 = base.first?.t, let n0 = noise.first?.t, let q0 = noise.first?.attitude, alpha != 0 else { return base }
        let nt = noise.map { $0.t - n0 }
        var j = 0
        return base.map { s in
            let t = s.t - b0 + offset
            while j + 1 < noise.count, nt[j + 1] <= t { j += 1 }
            guard t >= 0, t <= (nt.last ?? 0) else { return s }
            let n = noise[j]
            var out = s
            out.rotation = s.rotation + n.rotation * alpha
            out.accel = s.accel + n.accel * alpha
            let extra = Quat(rotationVector: (q0.conjugate * n.attitude).rotationVector * alpha)
            out.attitude = (s.attitude * extra).normalized
            out.gravity = extra.conjugate.rotate(s.gravity)
            out.pitch = s.pitch + (n.pitch - noise[0].pitch) * alpha
            out.yaw = s.yaw + remainder(n.yaw - noise[0].yaw, 2 * .pi) * alpha
            out.roll = s.roll + (n.roll - noise[0].roll) * alpha
            return out

lines: +Problem:

+Imagine: You have been a teacher for several years. You love interacting with students, and after long days at work, nothing brings you more joy than chatting with your partner and kids. But one day, your voice starts to fatigue. You struggle to articulate the words that used to come naturally.When the diagnosis for ALS comes, your whole life turns upside down. Suddenly, talking goes from something you used to love, to something you dread. As time goes by, it becomes harder and harder to form sentences, and you begin to feel disconnected from those around you.

+User(s): Unfortunately, this is one of the most common problems that people with ALS face. According to a 2011 review by Beukelman, Fager and Nordness (published in Neurology Research International and hosted on the NIH's PubMed Central), at some point 80 to 95% of people with ALS are unable to meet their daily communication needs using natural speech. Losing your ability to communicate doesn’t just make it harder for caretakers to understand your needs, it removes the very connection that you have with the people around you. Something as simple as telling your family you love them becomes an arduous task. Modern day eye-tracking technologies take far too long to generate sentences, which completely takes the user out of conversations and makes it seem artificial and non-human.

+Who LouVoice is for: people whose speech is getting slower or harder to understand, but who can still move their jaw the same way each time they say a word. ALS weakens the same jaw, lip and tongue muscles that LouVoice reads, so LouVoice works best when someone enrolls early, while those movements are still strong. Alex can still speak today, which makes now the best time for him to start.

+Our Solution + Core Loop: ElevenLabs(the world’s premier voice AI company) already has their impact program, that allows people with neurodegenerative diseases to create free clones of their voice, but the users still have to type words in to get the AI to speak them, which removes the personal element to a conversation because they have to actively type out their responses each time. The process is time consuming and artificial.

+LouVoice changes that. By using the built in sensors of standard Airpods, LouVoice tracks facial muscle movement and gets trained on the specific patterns that people use for words. Once that data is collected, simply moving your mouth will generate words on the dashboard that are read aloud by the ElevenLabs voice clone in your unique voice.
+How it works:
+Get set up. All you need is a pair of AirPods Pro 2 and a Mac. No special medical hardware.
+Create your voice. LouVoice builds a copy of your voice with ElevenLabs. (See Where your voice comes from below.)

+Teach LouVoice your words. Pick the words and phrases that matter most to you, like “I love you,” “how was your day,” or your kids’ names. Mouth each one a few times while wearing your AirPods. A first round of training takes about 10 minutes.
+Start talking. Mouth a word or phrase, and LouVoice shows it on screen and says it out loud in your own voice.
+Fix it in one tap. If LouVoice guesses wrong, you or a caregiver pick the right word from its top guesses. Every fix teaches it to do better next time.
+Grow with you. As your movements change, LouVoice notices which words are slipping and asks you to retrain just those, not start over.

+Building for patient’s needs: Deterioration over time is one of the biggest issues with ALS, so we want LouVoice to be able model the way your patterns change over time and adapt accordingly. This isn’t just a one-time use product, we want users to be able to use LouVoice for as long as they possibly can so that they can preserve their connections as long as possible.

+The physical limit: retraining can follow movements as they weaken, but only while they stay repeatable. Once the jaw can no longer move the same way twice, there is no pattern left for LouVoice to learn. Decline can also be fast: Beukelman et al. found that once intelligibility begins to decrease, speech performance often deteriorates so rapidly that there is little time to set up another way to communicate. LouVoice handles this in three ways:
+Enroll early. Training starts while movements are strong, so the model has a clean baseline to adapt from.

+Track and retrain word by word. Tiger Data stores each user's movement strength and per-word accuracy over time. When one word starts slipping, LouVoice asks the user to retrain just that word instead of starting over.

+Be honest when the signal fades. When movements become too weak to read reliably, LouVoice tells the user and their caregiver so they can plan the move to another communication method in time, instead of letting the app silently guess wrong.
+Where your voice comes from:
+LouVoice speaks in your voice, not a robotic one, and there are two ways to get it.

+If you can still speak: this is the best time to start. While you train LouVoice, you say each word out loud, and LouVoice records your voice at the same time. One session teaches LouVoice your movements and saves your voice for the future. If you’ve already lost some or all of your speech: your voice can be rebuilt from old recordings, like home videos, voicemails or recorded speeches. Family members can help find them. Through the ElevenLabs Impact Program, people living with ALS can get their voice clone for free.
+For caregivers:

+LouVoice is built for the person using it, but caregivers can help make it work day to day. Caregivers can: Help with setup: putting in the AirPods, creating the voice, and running the first training session. Turn listening on and off, so LouVoice only speaks when it’s meant to.
+Fix wrong words with one tap when the user can’t.
+Get early warnings. If LouVoice sees movements getting too weak to read reliably, it tells both the user and the caregiver, so there’s time to plan the next way to communicate together.
+Privacy and your data:
+Your voice and your movements are personal health information, and we treat them that way.
+Stays on your Mac: your raw movement data and your trained model.
+Goes to ElevenLabs: your voice recordings, only to create your voice clone.

+Goes to our servers only if you say yes: summary numbers about how your movements change over time (how strong they are, how accurate each word is), stored with Tiger Data to help LouVoice adapt to you.
+You’re in control: you can see what’s been shared and delete all of it at any time.
+LouVoice is a student project and hasn’t been through formal health-privacy certification yet.
+What LouVoice is not:
+Not a medical device. It hasn’t been clinically tested or approved, and it doesn’t replace a communication assessment from your ALS clinic or speech-language pathologist.
+Not mind-reading or open-ended speech. LouVoice only knows the words and phrases you’ve taught it.
+Not forever. LouVoice works as long as your mouth movements stay consistent. When they don’t, it will tell you honestly rather than guess.
+What you need
+AirPods Pro 2 (the model we’ve tested)
+A Mac running macOS 14 or newer
+An internet connection to set up your voice and to sync your progress (optional)
+About 10 minutes for your first training session

+Success test: For our MVP to be considered a success, the judge or the user should be able to speak each word to whatever their ability and train the model on that pattern. Once trained, the user mouths a full sentence and the ElevenLabs reads the words aloud with less than 1.5 seconds of delay. The product must feel conversational and real, not artificial, because that removes the very connection we are trying to preserve.
+How we measure it:
+Accuracy: word accuracy on a session the model never trained on. Today: 49% (default) to 68% (tuned) on 5 words, against 20% chance. Target: 90% or higher.
+Delay: time from the end of a mouthed word to the start of audio. Target: under 1.5 seconds.
+Sentence success: share of full sentences read out correctly. Today: about 15% for a 5-word sentence at 68% word accuracy.

+Biggest risks: The patient/user is unable to produce consistent movements for words so the model has to guess and get it wrong. The AI takes too long to read each word outloud, making it feel artificial. The model only registers one word at a time, so trying to speak a full sentence takes too long or doesn’t come out cleanly.

+Future developments: Use the generated text to be inputted into messages so the product works in the reverse: for people that have lost muscle function in their hands(cant type) but still have some voice capabilities.
